implementation_notes: C# 9 records with init-only properties and the with expression are the language's own test data builder: describe the record once with safe defaults (positional parameters with default values, or property initializers plus required members), then let a test write User.Valid() with { Email = "bad@example.com" } and mention nothing else. Object initializers cover non-record classes, required members turn a missing value into a compile error, and record copy semantics leave the base instance untouched. Write a hand-written builder only when construction is conditional or validated in a way a with expression cannot express; AutoFixture is the library form for large generated graphs.
pitfalls: with performs a shallow copy: nested reference-type members (collections, child objects) are shared with the original, so mutating them in a test corrupts the base instance for every later test.
Records compare by value across all fields, so an equality assertion over a record built from defaults asserts data the test never mentioned; override every field the assertion depends on.
The defaulted factory can drift from the production constructor's validation; keep ValidUser() calling the same constructor the application uses.

variants.name: AutoFixture Build<T>().With(...) over anonymous data
variants.implementation_notes: AutoFixture's own README describes it as offering a generic implementation of the Test Data Builder pattern: fixture.Build<User>().With(u => u.Email, "bad@example.com").Create() starts from an automatically populated, type-correct object graph and applies only the overrides the test names, while Create<T>() alone covers the cases where no field matters. Choose it when the graph is deep and hand-written defaults would be noisy, and add customizations/specimen builders so the generated data respects domain invariants instead of merely satisfying the type.
pitfalls: Anonymous data is type-valid, not domain-valid: without customizations a test can run against values the domain forbids, so the assertion may pass for the wrong reason.
Generated values depend on AutoFixture's strategies and change across versions, so any assertion that touches a non-overridden field turns brittle.
